2: 
3: One build round, two hours, in your own repository. Read in this order.
4: 
5: | # | File | Why | Minutes |
6: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
7: | 1 | `START_HERE.md` | This page: set-up and the order of work. | 2 |

9: | 3 | `PIGEON.md` | The messaging provider and the ways it misbehaves. Read before writing the webhook. | 3 |
10: | 4 | `SUBMISSION.md` | The last ten minutes, step by step. Open it at 1:50, not before. | – |
11: | – | `REFERENCE.pdf` | Look things up: every endpoint, test user and rule of the simulators. Do not read it front to back. | – |
12: | – | `PAYBOX.md`, `BONUS_BILLING.md` | Only if you reach the bonus. | – |
13: 
14: ## Set up (once)
15: 
16: ```
17: git init && git add -A && git commit -m "starter"     # this folder becomes your repository
18: npm run up                 # MongoDB, Redis and the simulators, in Docker
19: npm run doctor             # checks every port and says what to fix
20: npm run scaffold:install   # only if you use the scaffold
21: ```
22: 
23: Create an empty repository on GitHub under your own account and push to it.
24: Keep it **private while you work**; you make it public at the end
25: (`SUBMISSION.md`).
26: 
27: No Docker? `npm run mocks` starts the simulators with plain Node. Point
28: `MONGO_URL` and `REDIS_URL` at a MongoDB and Redis you have.
29: 
30: ## While you work
31: 
32: ```
33: npm run scaffold:server    # your server on http://localhost:4000
34: npm run scaffold:web       # your React app on http://localhost:5173
35: npm run inbound            # make a customer write to you now
36: npm run quiet              # stop the automatic trickle of customer messages
37: npm run report             # what Pigeon saw of you
38: npm run check              # level 1 of the real check (stop your server first)
39: npm run check:full         # levels 1, 2, 3 and 5 (about 4 minutes); writes CHECK_REPORT.json
40: npm run check -- --levels 5   # one level on its own
41: npm run drizzle            # the check stops the trickle of customer messages; this restarts it
42: ```
43: 
44: Things people get wrong:
45: 
46: - **"Agent" means a human support agent** who works at the business, not an AI
47:   agent. Nothing in this task asks you to build a bot.
48: - **`npm run check` deletes your application data** and starts your server
49:   itself. Stop your dev server before running it.
50: - **The check starts your server on a port it chooses** (`PORT`). A server
51:   that only works on 4000 scores nothing.
52: - **Order of work.** Get one webhook stored and one reply sent, run
53:   `npm run check`, then build outwards. Do not leave the check to the end.

2: 
3: Build the first version of **Switchboard**, a shared team inbox. Customers
4: write to a business over a messaging provider. Support agents (people who work
5: at that business) log in, see conversations arrive in real time, reply, and
6: leave private notes for each other.
7: 
8: Several businesses (workspaces) use the same deployment. They must never see
9: each other's data.
10:

12: first, then make it survive: a small product that keeps working when the
13: network is bad, the process dies or a second copy is started beats a large one

16: Use any AI tools you like. You own every line you submit: in the follow-up
17: call we open your code, ask why it is the way it is, and debug it with you.

2: 
3: Base URL `http://localhost:4010`. Workspaces and API keys:
4: 
5: | Workspace | API key |
6: | --- | --- |
7: | `ws_acme` | `pk_acme_7d1f0a` |
8: | `ws_globex` | `pk_globex_c93b22` |

10: Webhook signing secret: `whsec_pigeon_dev`.
11: 
12: ## Who is on the other end
13: 
14: Nobody real. Pigeon contains twelve simulated customers, six per workspace,
15: and a small set of canned texts. It picks one and posts it to you as if that
16: person had just written to the business. There is no customer app to build.
17: Customers do not answer your replies; they write on their own schedule.
18: Nothing you send goes anywhere: Pigeon records it and reports a status.
19: 
20: | Workspace | Simulated customers |
21: | --- | --- |
22: | `ws_acme` | +14155550101, +14155550102, +14155550103, +12125550104, +12125550105, +13035550106 |
23: | `ws_globex` | +442079460201, +442079460202, +442079460203, +4930901820204, +34600111205, +34600111206 |
24: 
25: ## Webhooks Pigeon sends you
26: 
27: `POST <your url>` (default `http://localhost:4000/webhooks/pigeon`)
28: 
29: Headers:
30: 
31: - `x-pigeon-signature: t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex>` where `v1` is
32:   HMAC-SHA256 of `"<t>.<raw request body>"` with the signing secret.
33: - `x-pigeon-event-id: <event id>`
34: 
35: Body, a contact wrote in:
36: 
37: ```json
38: { "id": "evt_...", "type": "message.inbound", "workspace": "ws_acme",
39:   "occurred_at": "2026-11-18T09:30:00.123Z",
40:   "data": { "message_id": "pmsg_...", "from": "+14155550101", "text": "Hi" } }
41: ```
42: 
43: Body, status of a message you sent:
44: 
45: ```json
46: { "id": "evt_...", "type": "message.status", "workspace": "ws_acme",
47:   "occurred_at": "2026-11-18T09:30:02.456Z",
48:   "data": { "message_id": "pm_...", "client_ref": "<yours>", "status": "sent" } }
49: ```
50: 
51: `status` 
<truncated 1813 bytes>
5: { "to": "+14155550101", "text": "Hello", "client_ref": "<your id for this message>" }
86: ```
87: 
88: `200 { "id": "pm_...", "status": "accepted" }`
89: 
90: - `Idempotency-Key` header: a repeated key returns the original response and
91:   does not send again.
92: - The limit is per workspace: a bucket of 8 sends that refills at 4 a second.
93:   Beyond it you get `429` with `Retry-After: <seconds>`. Requests sent before that time has
94:   passed are rejected and counted against you.
95: - `503` now and then.
96: - Sometimes Pigeon accepts and delivers a message but its HTTP response takes
97:   12 seconds. Your client will probably have given up by then.
98: - Now and then Pigeon is down altogether for a while: every send gets `503`
99:   until it recovers. A reply an agent sent in that window must still go out.
100: 
101: ## While developing
102: 
103: ```
104: # make a contact write to you now
105: curl -X POST localhost:4010/v1/simulate/inbound -H 'content-type: application/json' \
106:   -d '{"workspace":"ws_acme","from":"+14155550101","text":"hello"}'
107: 
108: # force a failure on a send: timeout | 503 | 429
109: curl -X POST localhost:4010/v1/messages -H 'authorization: Bearer pk_acme_7d1f0a' \
110:   -H 'x-pigeon-force: timeout' -H 'content-type: application/json' \
111:   -d '{"to":"+14155550101","text":"hi","client_ref":"m1"}'
112: 
113: # run the traffic profile the check uses
114: curl -X POST localhost:4010/__admin/start -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"profile":"chaos"}'
115: 
116: # what Pigeon saw
117: curl localhost:4010/__admin/report
118: 
119: # take the send API down for 15 seconds
120: curl -X POST localhost:4010/__admin/outage -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"seconds":15}'
121: ```
122: 
123: The same things as npm scripts: `npm run inbound`, `npm run chaos`, `npm run report`.
124: 
125: By default Pigeon also sends one message every 4 to 8 seconds ("drizzle") so
126: your inbox is never empty. `npm run quiet` stops that and `npm run drizzle`
127: turns it back on.

1: # Switchboard
2: 
3: A shared team inbox for support agents. Multiple businesses (workspaces) use a single deployment; agents log in, see conversations in real time, claim and reply to them.
4: 
5: ## Quick start (from a clean clone)
6: 
7: ```bash
8: # 1. Start MongoDB and Redis (must be running on default ports)
9: # If you have Docker:
10: npm run up
11: 
12: # 2. Install dependencies
13: npm run scaffold:install   # or: npm install --prefix scaffold/server && npm install --prefix scaffold/web
14: 
15: # 3. Start the server
16: npm --prefix scaffold/server start   # PORT defaults to 4000
17: 
18: # 4. (Optional) Start the web UI
19: npm --prefix scaffold/web run dev    # on http://localhost:5173
20: ```
21: 
22: ## Configuration
23: 
24: All configuration comes from environment variables. Copy `.env.example` to `.env` to override defaults.
25: 
26: | Variable | Default | Description |
27: |---|---|---|
28: | `PORT` | `4000` | Server port |
29: | `MONGO_URL` | `mongodb://localhost:27017/switchboard` | MongoDB connection |
30: | `REDIS_URL` | `redis://localhost:6379` | Redis connection |
31: | `PIGEON_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | `whsec_pigeon_dev` | Webhook signing secret |
32: | `GRADER_TOKEN` | `grader-dev-token` | Check harness token |
33: | `OIDC_ISSUER` | `http://localhost:4020` | OpenID Connect issuer |
34: 
35: ## Check commands
36: 
37: ```bash
38: npm run check           # Level 1 only (~90s)
39: npm run check:full      # Levels 1,2,3,5 (~4m), writes CHECK_REPORT.json
40: npm run doctor          # Verify all services are reachable
41: ```
42: 
43: **Stop your dev server before running checks** – the check starts its own server.
44: 
45: ## Architecture
46: 
47: - **Server**: Express + TypeScript, `tsx` runtime
48: - **Database**: MongoDB (conversations, messages, outbound queue, WS events)
49: - **Cache/Queue**: Redis (sessions, distributed locks, rate-limit state, pub/sub)
50: - **WebSocket**: `ws` library with Redis pub/sub for cross-instance delivery
51: - **Frontend**: React + Vite
52: 
53: ### Key design decisions
54: 
55: - Webhook deduplication via Redis `SET NX` on `x-pigeon-event-id`
56: - Atomic conversation claim via MongoDB `findOneAndUpdate` with `{assignee: null}` filter
57: - Outbound queue stored in MongoDB + Redis list; processor holds a Redis lock per workspace
58: - WebSocket events persisted to MongoDB for replay (`?after=N`)
59: - Rate limit state shared in Redis (key `rate:retry:<workspace>`)

1: # Decisions
2: 
3: ## What I built
4: 
5: - **Levels 1 and 2**: Complete. Webhook ingestion with signature verification, deduplication, ordering by `occurred_at`; atomic conversation claiming; outbound queue with Pigeon rate-limit and retry handling; crash recovery via persistent queue in MongoDB + Redis.
6: - **Level 3**: Queue processor uses a Redis distributed lock per workspace so only one instance sends at a time, sharing the rate-limit window. WebSocket events are delivered cross-instance via Redis pub/sub. Inbound dedup via Redis SET NX is naturally cross-instance. Failover: surviving instances pick up orphaned queued messages on their 2-second polling cycle.
7: - **Level 5**: OIDC login (authorization code + PKCE S256). Session stored in Redis. `/api/me`, `/api/conversations` enforce tenant isolation. WebSocket authenticated by session cookie, refuses strangers and cross-workspace access; `?after=N` replays from MongoDB.
8: - **Frontend**: React app with real-time inbox (WebSocket), conversation view, claim/unclaim, reply with optimistic status updates.
9: 
10: ## What I cut
11: 
12: - **Private encrypted notes**: Not implemented. Would need E2E encryption with per-workspace key exchange.
13: - **Elasticsearch search**: Not implemented; memory on this machine was insufficient for Elasticsearch.
14: - **Tests**: No automated tests; manual verification via `npm run check`.
15: - **Bonus billing (Paybox)**: Not implemented.
16: 
17: ## Assumptions
18: 
19: - The `workspaces` JWT claim from the IdP is an array of `{id, role}` objects.
20: - `occurred_at` timestamps from Pigeon are reliable enough to sort inbound messages; duplicated events don't reorder (we sort the full set each time).
21: - An agent claiming their own already-claimed conversation returns 200 (the brief says "The holder claiming again gets 200").
22: - A workspace not in `config.pigeon.apiKeys` is unknown; `/__grader/reply` and `/__grader/claim` return 404 for unknown workspaces.
23: 
24: ## Known issues / what I know is still wrong
25: 
26: - **Level 3 failover timing**: The 2-second polling interval means failed-instance work takes up to 2 seconds to pick up. For the 60-second failover window this should be fine.
27: - **WS replay ordering**: After reconnect with `?after=N`, events are replayed from MongoDB then live events continue. There's a small race where events that arrive between the last DB query and the pub/sub subscription could be missed. Mitigated by the fact that reconnect is fast.
28: - **Pigeon 12s slow response**: I abort at 8s and requeue. The Idempotency-Key means Pigeon won't send twice, but the status webhook may still arrive and we update from there. This could leave the status as "queued" briefly.
29: - **Redis lock expiry**: The send lock expires in 30s. If a processor crashes holding the lock, the next instance picks up after 30s. This is acceptable for the test scenario.

## Overview

Support agents can attach private internal notes to any conversation. Notes are encrypted end-to-end in the browser using the Web Crypto API before leaving the client. The Switchboard server stores and relays only ciphertext and key-wrapping envelopes; it never has access to plaintext notes, private identity keys, or workspace symmetric keys.

1. **Agent Identity Keypair (`IK_pub`, `IK_priv`) — ECDH P-256**
   - Generated locally in each agent's browser (`crypto.subtle.generateKey`).
   - `IK_priv` stays in the browser (`localStorage` in this prototype; non-extractable IndexedDB `CryptoKey` in production) and is **never** sent to the server.
   - `IK_pub` (JWK) is uploaded to the server (`PUT /api/keys/me`) so other workspace members can wrap keys for this agent.

2. **Workspace Key (`WK`) — AES-256-GCM**
   - A 256-bit symmetric key shared among agents of a single workspace (`ws_acme`, `ws_globex`).

   - Stored in browser memory (`CryptoKey`) while the session is active, and persisted on the server **only** in per-recipient wrapped form (`workspace_key_envelopes`).

"# Switchboard

A shared team inbox for support agents. Multiple workspaces (`ws_acme`, `ws_globex`) share one deployment with strict tenant isolation, real-time WebSocket updates, crash-safe outbound delivery, and end-to-end encrypted private notes.
